title: The Argument Game Works Well With Children (Valued Within Exercise)
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes a simple dinnertime activity he calls the Argument Game, which he uses to apply the Five Key Beliefs methodology from The Will to Learn at home with his own four children. In the game, a parent proposes a deliberately provocative statement (e.g., "chores should be optional") and children take turns, youngest to oldest, arguing against it -- a sequencing choice designed to give younger kids an easier entry point while pushing older kids to generate more sophisticated arguments. He frames the game as a Valued Within exercise because it has children construct their own reasons for family expectations rather than simply being told the reasons, while also building skill in earnest, amicable argumentation. Though written about his family, the piece is explicitly offered to educators as a portable, low-prep activity adaptable to classrooms, car rides, or extended family settings.
points: The Argument Game's mechanic -- youngest argues first, oldest last -- is a deliberate scaffolding choice that keeps younger children from feeling outmatched while still pushing older children toward novel reasoning.
Stuart explicitly classifies the activity as a Valued Within exercise: children construct their own justification for family rules rather than being told the reasons by a parent.
The game doubles as practice in "earnest and amicable argument," a skill Stuart treats as central to a flourishing life in his broader curriculum work.
He positions the activity as portable well beyond the dinner table -- usable with nieces, nephews, students, or on car rides -- making it a low-prep tool teachers can adopt directly.
quotes: A colleague asked me in the lunch line if I ever use the Five Key Beliefs methodology from The Will to Learn with my own children at home. The answer is yes, I do approach parenting with this lens, quite often.

Mom or Dad comes up with a statement the children are going to need to argue against. Sample statements we've used are: Chores should be optional for children, not mandatory. Children should be given anything they want.

The youngest to oldest thing is important because you want the older children to have to push harder to come up with novel arguments and you want the younger children to have a more open field within which to argue.

Thinking for themselves about why we have the expectations and rules in place that they sometimes don't like or value (so it's a Valued Within exercise); practicing the kind of earnest and amicable argument that makes for a flourishing life.
So whether you've got kids at home, or nieces and nephews, or even articulate pets, feel free to give it a try.
